content: 1. A significant reduction in new HIV cases among people who inject drugs aged 24 and younger was observed, with cases dropping from 771 in 2007 to 212 in 2013. 2. The Women for Women initiative was designed to provide gender-sensitive HIV and harm reduction services for women who inject drugs, female partners of people who inject drugs, and female ex-prisoners. Initially supported by UNODC, the program was transferred to municipal services in November 2013. 3. Six local NGOs received grants to integrate gender-sensitive approaches into their harm reduction services, offering comprehensive HIV and harm reduction services. These services included gender-based violence prevention (including counseling for male sexual partners), legal assistance, child care, hygiene and food supplies, shelter, self-esteem skill-building, and job placement. 4. Peer involvement was critical in delivering these services, and linkages were established with local government clinics and social services. The Women for Women initiative also facilitated ongoing dialogue between civil society organizations and local administrative structures to ensure the sustainability of these services. 5. Training for NGO staff and some government representatives included a study tour to Vienna to observe the daily operations of HIV and harm reduction services for women, as well as workshops on service development. Participants also received capacity-building in outreach techniques, leadership, empowerment, advocacy, and fundraising. 6. During the project grant period (2011–2012), 2,036 women accessed services through the program. The involvement of municipal service providers in harm reduction services for women in their communities helped reduce stigma and discrimination. 7. Financial sustainability was addressed by incorporating program activities into local service delivery structures. Intensive training ensured that NGO and government providers acquired the advocacy, management, and fundraising skills necessary for the long-term sustainability of these services. 8. In 2012, the Vietnam Authority of HIV/AIDS Control piloted a project to expand early access to HIV services for key populations, particularly people who inject drugs. This aimed to maximize the therapeutic and preventive benefits of antiretroviral therapy (ART) by enabling early treatment initiation. 9. The pilot project decentralized HIV testing and counseling (HTC) services from district facilities to commune health stations in Dien Bien and Can Tho provinces. Innovations included fixed-dose combination antiretroviral formulations, point-of-care HIV and CD4 testing, and decentralized follow-up. 10. Community partners, including peer educators, self-support groups, and village health-care workers, were actively engaged. They received community mobilization training and participated in regular meetings to discuss outreach activities and challenges. 11. Commune health station staff were trained in HIV service delivery, including rapid HIV testing, preand post-test counseling, adherence support, basic care, and dispensing antiretroviral drugs. This decentralized, community-based model promoted earlier diagnosis and treatment. 12. People diagnosed at commune health stations had significantly higher median CD4 counts when starting ART (median 294 cells/mm³) compared to those diagnosed at district facilities (median 88 cells/mm³). Community outreach and trust-building were recognized as critical for facilitating earlier access to HIV services among people who inject drugs. 13. Recognizing the acute risks faced by people in prisons and other closed settings, the Afghan Family Guidance Association (AFGA) provides comprehensive HIV prevention, treatment, and care services for female prisoners, with a focus on harm reduction for female injecting and non-injecting drug users in prison settings. 14. AFGA conducts advocacy through monthly meetings and awareness-raising events with government, legislative bodies, prison staff, and law enforcement to promote gender sensitivity and rights-based program approaches, reducing stigma and discrimination toward female injectors. 15. Support groups for female prisoners have been established, and peer educators for people who inject drugs have been trained in harm reduction approaches. Since 2008, AFGA has facilitated coordination between the Ministry of Public Health, prison officials, and the Ministry of Counter Narcotics to ensure vital health services are available to female prisoners and to identify injecting drug users for appropriate harm reduction services. 16. AFGA's coordination activities have significantly improved the prison health care delivery system and strengthened the referral network for female prisoners, including those who inject drugs. 17. In Albania, the NGO STOP AIDS implemented an incentives program targeting young people who inject drugs to assess whether small incentives could motivate reductions in high-risk behaviors associated with drug use and encourage safer alternatives. 18. Incentives included clean needles, returning used ones, HIV testing, bringing new clients to the program, and allowing home visits by STOP AIDS staff. Vouchers and coupons redeemable for retail goods were used as incentives, distributed weekly from a clinic-managed bank account. 19. The program significantly improved client attendance and uptake of harm reduction services, particularly needle and syringe programs (NSP), HIV and hepatitis testing, and introducing new clients and partners to the program. However, voucher incentives were less effective in changing behaviors such as returning used needles or switching from injecting to non-injecting behaviors. 20. Methadone maintenance treatment (MMT) for incarcerated injecting drug users was piloted in Kerobokan Prison, Bali, in 2005. The pilot project established comprehensive harm reduction services, including MMT, with high participation levels among prisoners with opioid dependence. 21. The program expanded MMT, education, care, support, and treatment services to 11 other prisons, detention centers, and parole services. Kerobokan Prison provides ongoing mentoring to these facilities. 22. High levels of integration with community health services in Bali ensure smooth transitions between prison and community MMT programs and early or continuing access to HIV treatment. HIV testing and treatment have been efficiently implemented in many prisons, with over 90% of high-risk prisoners tested and a high proportion of those testing positive starting ART. 23. In Iran, a concentrated HIV epidemic driven by injecting drug use led to advocacy efforts in 1996 targeting government, community, and religious leaders to shift from a zero-tolerance approach to harm reduction. The main strategy is opioid substitution therapy, primarily methadone maintenance treatment. 24. By February 2014, 4,275 drug treatment centers offered opioid substitution therapy under the supervision of medical science universities, state welfare organizations, or prison organizations. Over 95% of these centers are managed by private sector physicians. 25. In Ukraine, the All-Ukrainian Public Center Volunteer provides access to critical HIV prevention services for adolescents in juvenile detention. The program targets at-risk adolescents, including those registered with law enforcement and those incarcerated in juvenile detention centers. 26. The program includes capacity building for providers working with vulnerable adolescents to increase understanding of their needs, strengthen communication skills, and improve referrals to appropriate services. Training courses for working with vulnerable adolescents have been integrated into the professional development training plan for the Bila Tserkva Academy of the Criminal Executive Service of Ukraine. 27. In Cambodia, the SMARTgirl program aims to prevent and mitigate the impact of HIV and improve the sexual and reproductive health of entertainment workers, many of whom are sex workers. The program provides HIV prevention information, commodities, and referrals through trained peers. 28. SMARTgirl also supports harm reduction approaches, including counseling and linkages to methadone maintenance treatment and needle and syringe programs for entertainment workers who inject drugs. The program has worked to reduce stigma and discrimination by giving entertainment workers a voice at national and local levels. 29. In Accra, the SHARPER project recruited young female sex workers as peer educators to increase service uptake and engagement in care. Peer educators received training, supervision, and stipends to cover transportation and communication costs. They worked with 10–15 young female sex workers each month. 30. The program addressed challenges such as the chaotic and mobile lives of young female sex workers by offering peer-accompanied referrals to services and establishing linkages with organizations providing critical support, such as addressing human rights abuses, sexual violence, child care, and parenting skills.
